originalGroup.material:
Rehearsal Questions And Canal Gate · Reading

During rehearsals for our school concert, questions often arrived at the wrong moment. A singer would ask about next week's timetable while the pianist was trying to repeat a difficult passage. Nobody wanted questions to be unwelcome. We needed a way to give different questions a suitable time. ____1____ A problem affecting the passage being practised could be raised immediately; a question about another day could usually wait.

The conductor put a small box near the door for written questions. ____2____ A student who was afraid of forgetting something could write it down and return attention to the music. The box did not replace speaking when an answer was needed at once.

At the break, two volunteers grouped the notes by subject. ____3____ Five separate questions about the same meeting time could be answered together instead of taking five interruptions.

Some notes were too short to understand. “What about Friday?” could refer to a room, a song or a journey. ____4____ The conductor asked writers to include enough information for someone else to know what they meant.

By the following week, the box had become part of rehearsal. ____5____ It worked because the conductor read the notes and returned to unanswered questions, making the promise to listen visible.

While one group ____5____ (PREPARE) the brushes, another spread a covering over the path. We worked ____6____ (SLOW) so that the paint stayed on the surface we had been asked to cover. The supervisor checked each section before we moved on.

After ____7____ (FINISH), we put a sign beside the gate to show that the paint was still wet. It was more ____8____ (USE) than simply telling the people who happened to be there at the time.

The brushes ____9____ (CLEAN) in the place the supervisor had prepared. We returned them to their boxes and took ____10____ (WE) notes back to school. The project had involved more preparation and clearing up than the final photograph would show.

Game First Turn And Bus Poster · Reading

When our club introduced a new board game, the first explanation covered every rule in one long speech. New players nodded politely and then asked how to begin. ____1____ Hearing a complete list had not shown them how the first decisions fitted together.

For the next session, we prepared a small demonstration with only the pieces needed for one turn. ____2____ Players could see what changed when a piece moved instead of trying to imagine the whole game at once.

We still kept the full rule sheet on the table. A short demonstration could leave out an unusual situation, and someone might want to check the exact wording. ____3____ Simplifying the first step did not make the complete instructions unnecessary.

The demonstrator also left one choice for the newcomer to make. ____4____ If the experienced player made every decision, the lesson could look smooth while giving the learner no chance to connect a rule with a plan.

Photo Sequence And Postcode · Reading

Our class had fifty photographs of a bridge-building project but room for only six in the exhibition. We first chose the sharpest and most colourful images. The result looked attractive, yet it was difficult to tell what we had done. ____1____ A visitor could see a finished bridge without understanding the problem that had led to it.

We began again by writing the story in short steps. One photograph would show the original gap, another the materials and another a test. ____2____ The sequence needed images that explained different parts, not six versions of the same successful moment.

This meant keeping one picture that was not perfectly composed. It showed a support bending during an early trial. ____3____ Without that photograph, the later change in the design seemed to have appeared for no reason.

Captions were important too. A picture could show people holding a structure without explaining what they were checking. ____4____ We added the question being tested rather than simply listing everyone's name.

The final six were not the six photographs we liked most individually. ____5____ Together, they gave a reader a route through the work, including the point where our first idea had failed.

During a visit to another town, I went to the post office to send a parcel to my sister. The address ____1____ (WRITE) on a small card, but I had forgotten to copy the postcode. A worker asked me ____2____ (CHECK) it before filling in the final label.

I phoned my sister, ____3____ was waiting at home, and she read the full address slowly. I repeated each part ____4____ (CAREFUL) so that she could hear whether I had copied it correctly. The parcel was a birthday gift, and I did not want it to travel to the wrong place.

The worker showed me two delivery choices. One would arrive ____5____ (EARLY) than the other, but it cost more. She explained the difference without choosing for me. I decided on the service ____6____ matched the date I needed.

After ____7____ (PAY), I kept the receipt in my notebook. It included a number that could be used ____8____ (FOLLOW) the parcel's journey. My sister later sent a message saying that it had arrived.

When I returned home, I added the postcode to ____9____ (WE) family address list. The task had been simple only because someone had reminded me ____10____ (NOTICE) a missing detail before the parcel left.

New Student Tour And Old Desk · Reading

When I offered to show a new student around school, I planned the route I usually took each morning. It was fast and familiar to me. My teacher asked whether it would answer the questions a newcomer was likely to have. ____1____ Knowing the quickest route between my own lessons was not the same as knowing what someone else needed first.

I asked the student what she wanted to find. She mentioned the office, the library desk and a quiet place to eat her lunch. ____2____ Our first walk would be based on those needs rather than on every room I could name.

At each stop, I gave one useful detail and left time for a question. ____3____ A long speech while walking could make several places disappear into one stream of information.

I also used the names written on the doors. My friends called one room “the old workshop”, but its sign said “Art Room C”. ____4____ A nickname could help someone who already belonged to the group while confusing someone trying to follow a notice.

At the end, I asked the student to choose the way back to the office. ____5____ The point was to see which part of my explanation needed another example, not to judge how quickly she had learned the building.

A desk from the town's first school was brought to our museum last year. A retired teacher ____1____ (OFFER) to describe how pupils had used it. She asked us ____2____ (LOOK) at the small space beneath the writing surface.

The desk, ____3____ had once been shared by two pupils, was smaller than we had imagined. The teacher showed where books ____4____ (KEEP) during a lesson. She also explained that the scratches did not all come from the same time.

We listened ____5____ (ATTENTIVE) and wrote a short description. One student wanted to remove every mark from the desk so it would look new. The curator said that cleaning and changing an object were not always the same thing. We needed to decide ____6____ information might be lost.

After ____7____ (DISCUSS) the matter, we kept the visible marks and explained them. The display became more ____8____ (INTEREST) because visitors could connect the object with the people who had used it.

Before the exhibition opened, the retired teacher checked ____9____ (WE) wording. She corrected one detail about where pupils placed their bags. We were pleased ____10____ (HAVE) her account beside the desk, while making clear that it described one person's experience.

At our school craft fair, several items carried the word “reserved”. We thought the meaning was obvious until two buyers gave different explanations. One believed the item had already been paid for. The other thought it was being held for someone who had not yet decided. ____1____ A useful label needed to say which situation actually applied.

For unpaid holds, we added a time at which the reservation would end. ____2____ A visitor returning later could see whether the item was still waiting for that person or had become available again.

For paid items awaiting collection, we used a different card. The buyer's details stayed on a private list behind the table. ____3____ People passing the stall needed to know the item was sold, not to read someone else's contact information.

Helpers also needed a shared record. A change of shift could leave the next volunteer with no memory of an earlier conversation. ____4____ We wrote down the item number, its status and any collection arrangement instead of relying on “the blue one over there”.

The cards were not the most decorative part of the fair, but they reduced repeated questions. ____5____ Clear information allowed the volunteers to spend more time talking about the objects and less time reconstructing promises.

Map Key And Beach Display · Reading

Our geography club made a map of places students used after school. We drew a different symbol for each kind of place and assumed the result would explain itself. A younger visitor looked at a cup symbol and asked whether it meant a café or a drinking-water point. ____1____ The picture had not carried the meaning we had intended on its own.

We added a key beside the map. Each symbol appeared with a short label, and the same symbol was used for the same kind of place throughout. ____2____ A reader should not have to learn a new meaning halfway across the page.

Some locations served more than one purpose. The community centre had a study room as well as a café. ____3____ We gave it both symbols instead of making one category hide the other.

We also checked the words in the key. “Community facility” sounded precise to us but did not tell the visitor what they could actually do there. ____4____ We replaced it with names such as “study room” and “sports hall”.

Before displaying the map, we asked students from another class to use it to find a place for a particular activity. ____5____ Their questions showed us which symbols and labels still needed attention before the map was treated as finished.

The display included a note about the place ____5____ the photograph had been taken. That mattered because the book's example came from another coast. We did not assume that every matching colour meant the same kind of animal.

After ____6____ (COMPARE) our records, we found that one location had been written ____7____ (CORRECT). The teacher helped us check it against the visit plan before we changed the caption.

The final display was ____8____ (INTEREST) than the first draft because it included our questions as well as our answers. Visitors were invited to tell ____9____ (WE) if they could offer a source for further reading. We were pleased ____10____ (LEARN) more without giving an uncertain guess the appearance of a fact.
